title: Quantum-enhanced mechanical sensing with machine-learning estimation
authors: Finn Müßigbrodt, Andraž Omahen, Q. Rumman Rahman, Giulio Corazza, Yiwen Chu, Matteo Fadel
abstract: Massive mechanical oscillators couple directly to forces, accelerations and gravity, making them attractive probes of new physics and of quantum mechanics at macroscopic scales. Pushing sensitivities beyond the standard quantum limit for signals of unknown phase requires non-Gaussian quantum states, whose metrological advantage has so far been confined to lighter systems such as trapped ions. Here we operate a microgram-scale acoustic mode of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator as a phase-insensitive quantum-enhanced sensor. A transmon qubit prepares the mode in Fock states of up to seven phonons by optimal control, and resolves its phonon-number distribution after interaction with a weak resonant signal. Bayesian analysis yields a Fisher information five times the vacuum value, a 7.0 dB gain in signal-amplitude sensitivity over any classical probe state, irrespective of its energy, currently limited by state preparation infidelities. We then train a neural network on the measured sensor response to perform Bayesian estimation without any analytical model of the system, showing the same sensitivity gain with half the systematic bias. Our results establish acoustic resonators prepared in non-Gaussian states as quantum-enhanced probes for high-frequency gravitational waves, dark matter and wave-function collapse.
summary: This research demonstrates quantum-enhanced sensing using a microgram-scale acoustic resonator coupled to a transmon qubit. By preparing the mechanical mode in non-Gaussian Fock states, the authors achieved a 7.0 dB improvement in signal sensitivity over classical limits. The use of machine learning for estimation further validates this quantum advantage in a robust, model-free manner.
main_problem: The paper addresses achieving quantum-enhanced mechanical sensing beyond the Standard Quantum Limit (SQL) for unknown phase signals using macroscopic mechanical oscillators.
main_result: They demonstrated a 7.0 dB sensitivity gain in signal-amplitude estimation using a microgram-scale acoustic resonator prepared in non-Gaussian Fock states, validated by both analytical and model-free neural network estimation.
method: The methodology combines optimal control for non-Gaussian state preparation, weak resonant signal interaction, and advanced Bayesian estimation techniques, including training a neural network for model-free parameter estimation.
model_or_system: The system is a microgram-scale acoustic mode of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator (HBAR) coupled to a transmon qubit (cQAD device). The sensing protocol involves preparing the mechanical mode in Fock states $|kangle$ and measuring its response to a weak resonant signal.
key_observables: Fisher information (achieving five times the vacuum value), signal-amplitude sensitivity gain (7.0 dB), and the phonon-number distribution.
important_parameters: Fock state number ($k \le 7$), signal amplitude ($d$), phonon loss rate ($\Gamma$), and the measurement time ($t$).
main_assumptions: The initial estimation relies on a parametrized model, which is improved by using a model-free neural network estimator to mitigate systematic bias from model mismatch.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the cQAD setup and sensing protocol, showing measured phonon-number populations for vacuum and $|4angle$ probes, and quantifying the quantum advantage via the squared Hellinger distance.
paper_structure: The paper moves from establishing the physical platform and Hamiltonian to detailing the sensing protocol (state preparation, weak signal interaction, readout). It then presents the quantitative results, comparing the achieved sensitivity gain against classical limits and demonstrating the robustness of the estimation using machine learning.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges quantum information theory (quantum metrology, non-Gaussian states) with macroscopic quantum systems (mechanical oscillators), providing a concrete, high-impact platform for testing fundamental quantum limits in condensed matter/AMO physics.
